arml-1997-power-03.prompt: *(Power Question 1997: cornered polyhedra.)* A *corner pyramid with apex $D$* is a tetrahedron $DABC$ in which $\triangle ABC$ is equilateral and $\triangle DAB$, $\triangle DBC$, $\triangle DAC$ are isosceles right triangles with the right angle at $D$ (it is a corner cut from a cube). A *cornered polygon* is: (a) an equilateral triangle with a corner pyramid attached on it, completely covering it; (b) a regular hexagon divided into six equilateral triangles, each covered by a corner pyramid; (c) a square to which is first attached a pyramid whose base is congruent to the square and whose faces are equilateral triangles, each triangular face then being covered by a corner pyramid as in (a); (d) the same construction with a regular pentagon. A *cornered polyhedron* is a polyhedron whose faces have been replaced by the corresponding cornered polygons. To *corner* a polyhedron means that the cornered faces do not overlap. The *base angle* of a cornered face is the angle at which the cornered face rises above an edge of the original face (for the cornered square this is $\angle FMP$ of problem 2(a)). Let $P$ be a right pentagonal prism whose $5$ lateral faces are congruent squares (its bases are regular pentagons of the same edge). Prove that it is possible to corner $P$; i.e., show that the cornered faces do not overlap. The proof may use calculator approximations.
arml-1997-power-03.answer: At every edge the dihedral angle of the prism plus the two base angles is less than $360^\circ$ (about $327^\circ$ at a square-square edge and $292^\circ$ at a square-pentagon edge).
arml-1997-power-03.reviewNote: The book's solution quotes about 91.113 degrees for the base angle of a cornered pentagon; recomputing gives about 92.1 degrees. The conclusion is unaffected (the bound used is 120 degrees).

A *cornered polyhedron* is a polyhedron whose faces have been replaced by the corresponding cornered polygons. The figure shows a squat polyhedron (its net, and the folded solid): a band of ten squares around its "equator" (so the band forms a right decagonal prism) capped above and below by regular pentagons, triangles and further squares. Prove that it is impossible to corner this polyhedron; that is, show that the cornered faces do overlap. The proof may use calculator approximations.
arml-1997-power-04.answer: At an edge $AB$ between two equatorial squares the dihedral angle is $144^\circ$ and the two cornered squares need $2\cdot109.47^\circ$, total $>360^\circ$.
